passages.happening:
Concerning the Ammonites, the LORD asks, ‘Has Israel no sons? Is he without heir? Why then has Milcom taken possession of Gad?’ (verse 1). So the days are coming when God will sound the battle cry against Rabbah of the Ammonites, and it will become a heap of ruins, and Israel will take back what was taken from it (verse 2). Heshbon and the villages of Rabbah are told to wail, for Milcom will go into exile with his priests and officials (verse 3).

Why boast of your valleys, faithless daughter, trusting in your treasures and saying no one will come against you (verse 4)? God will bring terror on them from every side, and they will be scattered with no one to gather them (verse 5). ‘Yet afterward I will restore the Ammonites from captivity,’ declares the LORD (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Ammon lay east of the Jordan around its capital Rabbah. After the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III carried off the Israelite tribes east of the Jordan in the 730s BC, Ammon moved into the land of Gad. That is the grievance of verse 1. Milcom was Ammon's chief god.

Ammon also played a part in Judah's last days. Its king Baalis sent Ishmael to murder Gedaliah (40:14).

The judgment on Ammon ends with a promise of restoration, as Egypt's and Moab's did.
passages.later: Amos had already spoken against Ammon's violence (Amos 1:13). Chronicles records that the eastern tribes were carried off by ‘Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria’ (1 Chronicles 5:26).
passages.asks: Ammon trusted its treasures and said no one would come against it. Ask what you trust that makes you feel no one can touch you. And ask what it means that God still promises a future to those he judges.

passages.happening:
Concerning Edom: ‘Is there no longer wisdom in Teman? Has counsel perished from the prudent?’ (verse 7). The people of Dedan are told to flee, for God will bring disaster on Esau (verse 8). God will strip Esau bare and uncover his hiding places (verse 10). ‘Abandon your orphans; I will preserve their lives. Let your widows trust in Me’ (verse 11).

If those who did not deserve the cup must drink it, Edom will not go unpunished (verse 12). Bozrah will become a ruin (verse 13). A messenger has been sent among the nations to gather against Edom (verse 14). ‘The terror you cause and the pride of your heart have deceived you, O dwellers in the clefts of the rocks’ (verse 16). Though Edom builds its nest as high as the eagle, God will bring it down (verse 16).

Edom will become a horror like Sodom and Gomorrah (verses 17 and 18). Like a lion coming up from the Jordan's thickets, God will chase Edom from its land (verse 19). The heart of Edom's warriors will be like a woman in labor (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Edom lay south and east of the Dead Sea, in rugged mountains with towns cut into the rock. Teman was a region of Edom known for wise men; Job's friend Eliphaz came from there. Bozrah was one of its chief cities.

Edom traced its line to Esau, Jacob's brother, and the prophets remembered with special grief its conduct when Jerusalem fell. Much of this passage closely matches the book of Obadiah.

Verse 11 is a surprising word inside the judgment: God himself will keep Edom's orphans alive, and its widows may trust in him.

Edom here is an ancient nation. These notes identify no people or nation of the present day with Edom.
passages.later: Obadiah says almost the same: ‘The pride of your heart has deceived you, O dwellers in the clefts of the rocks’ (Obadiah 1:3). Amos foresaw even ‘the remnant of Edom’ among the nations who bear God's name (Amos 9:12), and James quotes that hope in Acts 15:17.
passages.hard:
Why does God promise restoration to Ammon and Elam but not to Edom?

The chapter treats the nations differently. Ammon (verse 6) and Elam (verse 39), like Egypt (46:26) and Moab (48:47), receive a promise of restoration, while Edom's ruin is described as lasting (verse 13). Some readers see this as a reflection of Edom's particular guilt, above all its violence against its brother Judah when Jerusalem fell. Others note that Old Testament language of lasting ruin often describes a nation's political end, which did come for Edom as a kingdom, rather than the fate of every person descended from it. Still others point out that the prophets elsewhere see even Edom's remnant gathered in (Amos 9:12, cited in Acts 15:17 of the nations).

Verse 11 itself promises care for Edom's orphans and widows. These notes identify no present-day people with Edom, and the passage gives no one a warrant to wish ruin on any people now.
passages.asks: Edom's pride deceived it into thinking it was out of reach. Ask where pride has made you feel safe from God. And ask what it means that even in judgment God promises to keep the orphans alive.

passages.t: Damascus, Kedar and Hazor, and Elam
passages.happening:
Concerning Damascus: Hamath and Arpad are ashamed at bad news; they are troubled like the sea (verse 23). Damascus has become weak and turned to flee; panic has seized her (verse 24). Her young men will fall in her streets (verse 26), and God will set fire to her walls (verse 27).

Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor, which Nebuchadnezzar struck: the order is to rise up and attack Kedar and destroy the people of the east (verse 28). Their tents, flocks and camels will be taken (verse 29). They must flee and hide (verse 30). Nebuchadnezzar has made a plan against a nation at ease, living securely, without gates or bars (verse 31).

Concerning Elam: ‘Behold, I will shatter Elam’s bow, the mainstay of their might’ (verse 35). God will bring the four winds against Elam and scatter its people (verse 36). He will set his throne in Elam (verse 38). ‘Yet in the last days, I will restore Elam from captivity,’ declares the LORD (verse 39).
passages.hearers:
Damascus was the capital of Aram, and Hamath and Arpad were cities to its north in Syria. By Jeremiah's day they had long since fallen under Assyria and then Babylon.

Kedar was an Arab tribe of the desert, and the kingdoms of Hazor here are probably desert settlements, not the old city of Hazor in Galilee. Their people lived in tents with flocks and camels, unwalled and at ease.

Elam lay far to the east, beyond Babylon, in what is now southwest Iran, around its city Susa. To break its bow was to break the source of its strength.

The chapter ends with a promise of restoration for the farthest nation on the list.
passages.later: Isaiah pictured Elam's bowmen: ‘Elam takes up a quiver, with chariots and horsemen’ (Isaiah 22:6). Amos had spoken against Damascus a century before (Amos 1:3-5).
passages.asks: The desert peoples lived at ease without gates or bars. Ask what security you rely on that would vanish in a day. And ask what it means for you that God's word reaches even the farthest nation with a promise.
